title: Stop Vibe Coding. Start Writing Specifications.
summary: Why a clear specification matters when you write code with AI.

children: "Code is the implementation. The specification is the product."

Why document requirements when AI can generate hundreds of lines of code in seconds?

title: What Makes Redis Special? Understanding Why a Single-Threaded Database Can Handle Massive Scale
summary: A closer look at how Redis handles work at scale.

children: If you've worked with backend systems, chances are you've heard Redis being described as "just a cache."
The reality is that Redis is much more than that.

Redis is an open-source in-memory data structure store that can be used as a database, cache, message broker, and streaming engine. Over the years, it has become one of the most widely adopted infrastructure technologies because of its flexibility, simplicity, and performance.
What makes Redis fascinating is not just what it does, but how it does it.
The concept of atomicity in Redis
Why Redis can support a massive number of concurrent connections while remaining incredibly fast
Most developers first encounter Redis as a caching solution.
While caching is one of its most popular use cases, Redis offers far more capabilities.
Redis provides several powerful data structures out of the box:
These data structures allow developers to build a wide variety of applications without reinventing common data storage patterns.
This flexibility is one of the biggest reasons behind Redis' exponential growth in popularity.
Instead of being limited to a single use case, Redis becomes a general-purpose building block that fits naturally into many architectures.
The Most Important Property of Redis: Atomicity
Among all the features Redis provides, one characteristic stands out above everything else:
To understand why this matters, consider a situation where multiple clients are connected to Redis simultaneously.
Suppose one command is currently executing.
Redis guarantees that this command will run to completion before another command begins execution.
The execution is never interrupted midway.
There is no situation where Redis pauses one command, executes another command, and then comes back.
The command runs completely before the next one starts.

This greatly simplifies application development because developers don't need to constantly worry about concurrent modifications.
Let's assume the value of a key is currently:
Now imagine ten clients simultaneously execute:
In many systems, concurrent updates can lead to race conditions.
But in Redis, every increment operation executes atomically.
As a result, the final value will always be:
This guarantee is one of Redis' most powerful features.
Another major reason behind Redis' speed is that it stores data in memory.
Unlike traditional databases that frequently access disk storage, Redis performs operations directly on memory-resident data structures.
Memory access is dramatically faster than disk access.
This is why Redis became the default caching solution for so many applications.
However, Redis is not limited to being a cache.
A common misconception is that Redis can only store temporary data because everything lives in memory.
In reality, Redis provides multiple persistence mechanisms.
Redis allows developers to configure how data should be persisted.
Redis can periodically dump the contents of memory to disk.
This means that even if the Redis process crashes, it can restart using the latest snapshot rather than starting from scratch.
Redis also supports write-ahead logging through an Append Only File.
Every update command executed by Redis can be recorded sequentially in a log file.
This log can later be replayed to reconstruct the database state.
This flexibility allows Redis to serve different workloads with different durability requirements.
Additional Features That Make Redis Powerful
Beyond performance and atomicity, Redis includes several capabilities that are commonly required in modern systems.
Redis supports transactions, allowing multiple operations to execute together.
Redis can act as a lightweight messaging system.
A publisher sends messages to a topic, and all subscribers listening to that topic automatically receive those messages.
This enables event-driven architectures and real-time communication systems.
Redis allows expiration times to be attached to keys.
This automatically deletes the key after 30 minutes.
When memory limits are reached, Redis can automatically evict keys based on configurable strategies.
This prevents applications from crashing due to memory exhaustion.
Now let's address the most interesting question.
How does Redis handle large numbers of clients?
Suppose you have a database server receiving requests from thousands of users.
A traditional solution would be to create a separate thread for each connection.
This is the classic multi-threaded model.
At first glance, this seems ideal because multiple requests can execute simultaneously.
However, this introduces a major challenge:
This is the classic race condition problem.
These synchronization mechanisms ensure correctness but introduce additional overhead.
Threads that are ready to execute often spend time waiting.
Instead of relying on multiple threads for command execution, Redis uses a model called:
This is the foundation of Redis' architecture.
To understand I/O Multiplexing, we first need to understand a problem with network communication.
Suppose a server wants to read data from a socket.
The problem is that read operations are typically blocking.
If no data has arrived yet, the thread simply waits.
During this waiting period, the CPU is doing nothing useful.
In highly concurrent systems, this becomes inefficient.
Instead of immediately reading from every socket, Redis first asks:
Which sockets currently have data available?
The operating system provides mechanisms such as:
These allow Redis to monitor large numbers of connections efficiently.
Redis only attempts to read from sockets that are ready.
This is the essence of I/O Multiplexing.
At the center of Redis is a single-threaded event loop.
The loop continuously performs four activities:
Everything happens within a single thread.
There are no worker threads executing commands in parallel.
There are no locks protecting data structures.
There are no mutexes around every operation.
The event loop simply processes requests one after another.
Because command execution is extremely fast, Redis can move through requests at a remarkable rate.
This is where Redis makes a crucial observation.
Receiving data from clients takes time.
the actual work is usually just an in-memory operation.
Adding an element to a list.
Redis therefore spends most of its time waiting for network activity, not executing commands.
Redis achieves very high throughput while avoiding the complexity of traditional multi-threaded architectures.
Redis is often associated with caching, but its capabilities extend far beyond that.

Its rich set of data structures, atomic command execution, in-memory architecture, configurable persistence mechanisms, Pub/Sub capabilities, transactions, TTL support, and efficient handling of concurrent connections make it one of the most versatile pieces of infrastructure in modern applications.
Perhaps the most interesting aspect of Redis is that many of these capabilities are built on a surprisingly simple execution model.

By combining a single-threaded event loop with I/O Multiplexing and extremely fast in-memory operations, Redis is able to deliver high throughput while avoiding much of the complexity typically associated with highly concurrent systems.
Understanding these design choices not only helps in using Redis more effectively, but also provides valuable insight into how modern high-performance systems are engineered.
The next time you use Redis for caching, it's worth remembering that behind a simple GET or SET lies one of the most elegant and influential system designs in modern software engineering.

title: What a Message Queue Really Is
summary: A plain-language look at message queues and where they fit in a distributed system.

children: In this article, we will break down what a message queue really is by designing one from first principles and understanding the constraints that shape real-world systems.

Message queues are a fundamental building block in distributed systems. We interact with them through APIs, configurations, and operational dashboards, but rarely pause to examine the assumptions they make about failure, ownership, and time.

Instead of starting with a specific technology, this article takes a bottom-up approach. We will build a message queue layer by layer. Each layer introduces a new constraint that breaks our previous design and forces us to rethink how the system should behave. The goal is not to implement a production system, but to understand the reasoning that makes real message queues look the way they do.
Layer 0: The Simplest Possible Message Queue
At its core, a message queue consists of three actors:
The queue is a simple FIFO list.
Enqueue: a producer appends a message to the queue
Dequeue: a consumer removes the message at the front
Once a message is dequeued, the system assumes it is processed. There is no tracking, no retries, and no acknowledgements.

This design preserves FIFO ordering and is easy to reason about. However, if a consumer crashes after dequeuing a message, that message is lost permanently. The queue has no knowledge of who took it or whether it was processed.

figure.alt: One message producer publishes to a topic that sends messages to three consumers.

children: Now we introduce a single real-world constraint. A consumer can crash after receiving a message.
With this change, deleting a message at delivery time is unsafe. Delivery and completion must be treated as separate events.
Messages now move through explicit states:
This introduces acknowledgements. A consumer must explicitly signal that it has successfully processed a message before the queue can delete it.
Track which messages are currently in flight
Track which consumer owns each message
Decide what to do if a consumer disappears
Ready queue containing messages available for delivery
If an acknowledgement never arrives, the message is not complete and must eventually beretried.

figure.alt: Three examples of consumers acknowledging messages, with message status shown at each step.

children: When a consumer crashes, the queue must reclaim its in-flight messages. A key design question arises. Where should failed messages be placed?
This prioritizes earlier messages but risks repeated retries blocking the entire queue.
This allows other messages to progress but weakens strict FIFO guarantees.
These mechanisms prevent individual messages from degrading overall system throughput.

figure.alt: A delivery failure reroutes a message from its original channel to a dead-letter channel.

children: Introducing acknowledgements leads to several unavoidable outcomes.

If a consumer processes a message but crashes before acknowledging it, the message will be redelivered. This results in at-least-once delivery semantics and requires consumers to handle duplicates safely.
The queue cannot know with certainty whether a consumer is dead or merely slow. It infers state using timeouts, heartbeats, or connection status.
Reclaiming messages too early increases duplicates. Waiting too long reduces throughput. Timeout values are always approximations.
At this point, a key insight becomes clear.
Message queues are not primarily about storing messages. They are about tracking responsibility.
Acknowledgements encode more than completion. They implicitly answer:
Whether the acknowledgement is still valid
With long-lived connections, message ownership can be tied directly to the connection. If the connection drops, ownership is revoked automatically and in-flight messages are reclaimed.
With stateless protocols, acknowledgements can arrive after the queue has already assumed the consumer is inactive. This complicates ownership validation and recovery logic.
Transport choices therefore directly affect correctness, not just performance.
We now allow multiple consumers to pull from the same queue.
The message lifecycle remains unchanged, but ownership is distributed.
The queue must now answer new questions:
How are messages assigned to consumers?
How many messages can one consumer hold at a time?
What does fairness mean in this system?
At this stage, the queue becomes a scheduler rather than a simple dispatcher.

figure.alt: Two producers send messages to a broker, which forwards them to two consumers.

children: If consumers can pull messages without limits, fast consumers can monopolize the queue while slow consumers starve.
A common solution is credit-based delivery. Each consumer is allowed a fixed number of in-flight messages. Messages are delivered only when credit is available, and acknowledgements free that credit.
This introduces backpressure and prevents unbounded message accumulation.
The queue can still deliver messages in FIFO order. However, once messages are processed concurrently, completion order is no longer guaranteed.
Delivery order and processing order are fundamentally different concepts in concurrent systems. Understanding this distinction is essential when designing consumers.
Distinguishing between a slow consumer and a failed one is one of the hardest problems in message queue design.
As long as the consumer’s connection is alive, it is considered active. If the connection drops, in-flight messages are reclaimed immediately.
Messages become invisible for a fixed duration. If no acknowledgement arrives within that window, the message becomes available again.
Short timeouts increase duplicate processing. Long timeouts reduce throughput. There is no perfect value, only informed tradeoffs.
By building a message queue from first principles, we can see how complexity emerges naturally from simple constraints.

Ignoring failures allows for simple designs but breaks immediately in real systems. Handling consumer failure introduces acknowledgements and ownership tracking. Supporting multiple consumers transforms the queue into a scheduler where fairness, flow control, and backpressure matter.
Across all layers, the core responsibility of a message queue remains constant.
It must track who owns a message at any point in time and safely reclaim that ownership when things go wrong.
When viewed through this lens, the architecture of message queues becomes easier to reason about, and their design decisions start to feel inevitable rather than arbitrary.

title: Understanding Apache Kafka and Its Role in Modern System Design
summary: An introduction to Apache Kafka and its place in modern system design.

children: When building large scale applications, one of the biggest challenges is handling data reliably and in real time. As systems grow, direct communication between services becomes difficult to manage, scale, and maintain. Apache Kafka addresses this challenge by enabling systems to communicate through events instead of direct calls.
Apache Kafka is widely used in modern backend systems to build scalable, fault tolerant, and real time data pipelines.
Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed to publish, store, and process streams of data in real time. It allows multiple systems to produce and consume events asynchronously.

Instead of one service directly calling another, Kafka acts as an intermediary where events are written once and consumed by multiple systems independently. This design improves scalability and system reliability.
A producer is responsible for sending data to Kafka. Producers publish events to specific topics without needing to know which services will consume them.
A topic represents a stream of events. All messages related to a particular domain or feature are stored under a topic.
Topics are divided into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, immutable sequence of records. Partitions allow Kafka to scale horizontally and handle large volumes of data efficiently.
Consumers read data from topics. They can be grouped into consumer groups to distribute the load and process data in parallel.
A broker is a Kafka server that stores data and serves read and write requests from producers and consumers.
When a producer sends data, it is written to a topic partition on a broker. The data is stored on disk and replicated across multiple brokers to ensure fault tolerance.

Consumers read data by maintaining offsets, which indicate how much data has already been processed. This allows consumers to replay data if needed, making Kafka suitable for both real time and batch processing use cases.
High throughput messaging with low latency
These characteristics make Kafka a strong foundation for event driven systems.
Consider an online food delivery platform handling thousands of orders per minute.
When a user places an order:
The order service publishes an event to Kafka
The payment service consumes the event and processes payment
The delivery service assigns a delivery partner
The notification service sends updates to the user
The analytics system records the event for reporting
Each service operates independently, and failures in one service do not block others. Kafka ensures reliable event delivery across the system.
Supports multiple consumers for the same data
Allows replaying events for recovery and debugging
Requires operational expertise to manage clusters
Message ordering is guaranteed only within a partition
Overkill for small or simple applications
Kafka is a good choice when your system:
Needs high availability and fault tolerance
Has multiple independent services consuming the same data
For early stage applications or small systems, simpler messaging solutions may be more appropriate.

Apache Kafka enables a shift from tightly coupled systems to event driven architectures. It helps build scalable and reliable systems, but it should be adopted with a clear understanding of its complexity and operational requirements.
Used correctly, Kafka becomes a powerful backbone for modern distributed systems.

summary: Load-balancing algorithms explained through real-world examples.

children: When an application grows and serves thousands or even millions of users, managing the traffic effectively becomes crucial. This is where

comes in. Load balancing is the process of distributing incoming network traffic evenly across multiple servers. By doing this, no single server gets overloaded, ensuring smooth performance, reduced waiting times, and higher availability even when a server fails.
In this article, we’ll explore five important load balancing algorithms using clear examples, along with their advantages, disadvantages, and when to use each one.

Imagine a restaurant on a busy evening. Customers come in constantly. If all customers are sent to a single waiter, that waiter gets overwhelmed while others stand idle. A good manager distributes customers equally among all waiters. This way, no one is overworked, and service remains smooth.

Load balancing works similarly in computer systems. Requests from users are treated like customers and servers act like waiters. The load balancer ensures all servers handle requests fairly, based on a strategy called an algorithm.

figure.alt: Six clients send requests through one load balancer to three backend servers.

children: Round Robin is like dealing cards at a poker table. The dealer gives cards to each player one by one in a circular order. Similarly, in Round Robin, requests are sent to servers one after another in order. When the last server is reached, the next request goes to the first server again.
Use this when all servers are equally powerful and can handle similar loads.
Simple to understand and implement. Requests are distributed evenly.
It doesn’t consider if a server is already too busy. It simply follows the rotation.

Consider three identical food delivery kitchens. Orders are sent to Kitchen 1, then Kitchen 2, then Kitchen 3, and then back to Kitchen 1, regardless of how many orders are currently being cooked in each kitchen.

figure.alt: A load balancer receives requests from six clients and directs them to three servers.

children: Weighted Round Robin improves the basic Round Robin by giving preference to more powerful servers. Servers are assigned weights based on their capacity. A server with a higher weight receives more requests.
Use this when servers have different capabilities. You want stronger servers to handle more traffic.
Better use of server capacity. Stronger servers handle more load.
Slightly more complex than basic Round Robin. Still doesn’t consider real-time server load.

Three call centers receive support calls. Center A has 100 agents, Center B has 50, and Center C has 25. Using Weighted Round Robin, Center A gets more calls than B or C since it can handle more customers.

figure.alt: A load balancer routes incoming requests to three servers with different illustrated loads.

children: This method looks at how many active connections each server currently has. The next request is sent to the server with the fewest active connections.
Ideal when servers may receive tasks of different lengths or workloads. Helps prevent overloading a busy server.
Dynamically balances load based on current server activity.
Servers must track active connections. Less effective if servers differ in processing power.
Imagine valet parking staff. Cars are sent to the valet who currently has the fewest parked cars, ensuring no single valet gets overwhelmed.
This strategy measures how quickly each server is responding. Requests are sent to the server that is currently responding the fastest.
Best for systems where server performance varies due to workloads.
Reduces delays for users. Helps select the most responsive server.
Needs accurate response-time monitoring. May ignore current server load.
Think of multiple checkout counters at a supermarket. Customers prefer to go to the counter where people are moving fastest, even if some counters have fewer people.

figure.alt: Least-response-time routing compares time to first byte and active connections across backend servers.

children: The IP Hash method uses the user’s IP address to determine which server will handle their request. This ensures that requests from the same client always go to the same server, maintaining session consistency.
Useful when your application needs session persistence, meaning a user’s requests must always go to the same server.
Can result in uneven distribution if some clients generate more traffic. Needs adjustments if a server fails.
Imagine assigning each regular customer a specific waiter whenever they visit. This way, the waiter remembers their preferences and provides better service.

figure.alt: Clients route through a load balancer to backend servers labeled by relative CPU load.

children: Each algorithm serves a different purpose. If your servers are identical and you want simplicity, Round Robin works well. If your servers have different strengths, Weighted Round Robin is better. When workload varies dynamically, Least Connections or Least Response Time provide smarter distribution. If your system relies on session persistence, IP Hash is the way to go.

In real-world applications like e-commerce platforms, video streaming, or food delivery apps, selecting the right load balancing strategy can significantly improve both user experience and system efficiency.

Load balancing is an essential part of building scalable and reliable applications. By understanding how each algorithm works and where it fits best, developers and architects can design systems that handle growing traffic smoothly.
From simple Round Robin to intelligent Least Response Time, each approach plays a role in modern system design. I hope this detailed guide helps you choose the right strategy for your applications.

title: Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication
summary: Two ways services exchange requests and respond to one another.

children: In the world of software architecture, the way systems communicate plays a crucial role in their performance, scalability, and reliability. One of the most fundamental concepts in system design is understanding
. These two patterns determine how services interact, respond, and handle requests.
In this article, I will explain both communication types using real-world analogies, discuss their key features, advantages, disadvantages, and guide you on when to use each in your applications.
is a pattern where the sender sends a request and waits until the receiver processes the request and sends back a response. During this period, the sender is unable to perform other tasks.

Imagine standing at a ticket counter. You approach the counter, request a train ticket, and wait until the cashier checks availability, prints the ticket, and hands it to you. Only after receiving your ticket can you move on.
This is synchronous communication. Your task remains blocked until the response (your ticket) is received.
: The sender cannot continue until a response is received.
: Responses are instant after the processing completes.
: Both sender and receiver must be available at the same time for the process to succeed.
: Easier to develop and debug due to its straightforward, request-response pattern.
: Real-time error reporting and data retrieval.
: Ensures data consistency as actions occur sequentially.
: The sender remains idle while waiting for the response, potentially wasting processing time.
: As the number of requests grows, blocking behavior can reduce system throughput.
: Components rely on each other being available simultaneously, making the system less flexible.
: Real-time data fetches require synchronous interactions.
allows the sender to send a request and continue working without waiting for a response. The receiver processes the request independently and responds when ready.

Think of sending a package via courier. You drop off the parcel at the courier office and leave. The courier company delivers the package while you continue with your day. Once delivered, you might get a notification confirming delivery.
This is asynchronous communication. The sender does not wait and can perform other tasks while the receiver handles the request in the background.
: The sender continues processing without waiting for a response.
: The sender and receiver operate independently.
: The response may be received after a significant time gap.
: Systems can handle other tasks while waiting for responses.
: Suitable for handling large volumes of requests without bottlenecking.
: If one component fails temporarily, the system can still function.
: Since responses are delayed, tracking errors becomes harder.
: Ensuring consistency across distributed systems is more complex.
: Not suitable for tasks requiring immediate feedback.
: Sending emails without waiting for delivery confirmation.
: Generating reports or processing uploaded images.
: Handling thousands of incoming orders without blocking.
: Systems like SMS or push notifications.
Use synchronous communication when immediate results are required. Use asynchronous when delayed processing is acceptable.
If your system must handle millions of requests simultaneously, asynchronous is generally better.
If your components need to work independently, asynchronous communication is the right fit.
While asynchronous offers scalability, it introduces complexities like message ordering and delayed error detection.
Always evaluate how the communication type affects your end-user experience. For critical, real-time operations, synchronous is usually preferred.
Both synchronous and asynchronous communication patterns are essential tools in system design. Neither is universally better than the other. It all depends on your application's specific needs.

Synchronous communication is simple and direct but limits scalability due to its blocking nature. Asynchronous communication improves scalability and resource utilization but requires more sophisticated handling of tasks and errors.
As a developer or architect, understanding when to use each pattern is key to building robust, efficient, and scalable systems.

children: As applications scale globally, database architectures become central to performance, reliability, and user experience. A well-designed database architecture can be the difference between seamless access and frustrating delays. This article dives deep into one such architecture:

, with a special focus on their role in active-active deployments. We’ll explore what makes a database suitable for modern, global applications, evaluate different architecture models, and understand their trade-offs using practical, real-world examples and beginner-friendly analogies.
What is a Distributed Database Architecture?

is a system where the data is stored across multiple servers or physical locations, often spread across various regions or countries. The main goal of such systems is to ensure that users, no matter where they are, can access and interact with data quickly, reliably, and consistently.

Imagine you run a chain of bookstores. Rather than stocking every single book only in the main warehouse, you store popular titles in each city store so that local customers can get them quickly. Similarly, distributed databases replicate or partition data across locations so users aren’t always waiting for distant servers.

Think of a global hotel booking platform. During holiday seasons, users from Los Angeles, London, and Tokyo might all be making bookings at the same time. If all their requests go to a central database in Frankfurt, latency and system overloads can lead to timeouts. Instead, a distributed system places data closer to users and synchronizes changes across locations.
In modern systems, it's common to deploy applications in an
, meaning multiple data centers (or cloud regions) are live and accepting user traffic simultaneously. This provides:
, even if one data center fails
However, there's a common misconception: that an active-active setup
a multi-master database. This is not true, and as we’ll explore, such setups can introduce consistency issues that may harm user experience.
Four Key Requirements for Active-Active Databases
A database supporting an active-active setup must deliver:
– Reads and writes should occur locally for low latency.
– Data should persist even after hardware or network failures.
– Users should see up-to-date, accurate data everywhere.
– The system should stay functional during failures.
Because it’s difficult to excel in all four simultaneously, different architectures prioritize different trade-offs.
In this architecture, multiple nodes must agree before committing a write. If any node fails, the transaction is rolled back to maintain consistency.
Think of friends trying to order a group meal. Unless everyone confirms their order, no one gets food. It's safe but slow.
High latency, especially across global distances
Banking systems that prioritize data accuracy over speed.
All nodes can accept writes, which are then synchronized. Sounds ideal—until two writes conflict.
Imagine two editors making changes to the same paragraph in different copies of a book. Later, someone has to decide which version stays.
Hard to predict final state of data
A user in New York adds a phone to their cart while a system in London removes it due to stock changes. The final version may ignore one update entirely.
Here, the data is divided into partitions (called shards), and each shard has a primary node responsible for handling reads and writes for that data.
It’s like assigning different departments in a company to handle specific tasks. One handles HR, one handles sales. No overlap, so no confusion.
Needs smart routing of user requests to correct shard
In a ride-sharing app, users from Asia are routed to the Singapore shard while US users go to the Oregon shard. Both operate independently but remain consistent through replication.
Let’s say we have a shopping app with users from Europe and Asia. We set up:
with a primary node in Frankfurt

Each data center also hosts replicas of the other shard. So if Frankfurt goes down, Paris takes over in seconds. When a European user adds a product to their cart, the data is processed locally. The same applies to users in Asia. There’s no data clash, no inconsistency.

to ensure reads reflect durable data
MongoDB supports causal consistency. This means your app will always read its most recent writes, even if the reads and writes happen in different regions or servers.
It’s like editing a Google Doc from your phone and laptop. Even if you're switching devices, every update is visible in real time.

Choosing the right database architecture is vital for modern apps. While multi-master databases offer local writes, they often sacrifice consistency and predictability. Distributed transactions offer safety but lack performance. Sharded (partitioned) databases offer the best balance: performance, consistency, availability, and durability.

For developers and architects building global apps, understanding these trade-offs ensures better decisions and smoother experiences for users. MongoDB is a great example of how sharded architecture can power resilient, high-performing, active-active applications.

title: Database Indexes

children: In the world of software development and system design, performance is everything. Whether you’re building a small web app or a large-scale system with millions of users, how quickly your application can retrieve data matters a lot.
One of the most effective ways to speed up data access in databases is by using
Let’s understand this with a real-world scenario.

You walk into a large library with thousands of books and need to find a book about "Ancient Greek Architecture." Without any system in place, you'd have to browse every shelf and read every title until you find it very time-consuming and inefficient.
But with a catalog or index system, you simply search for your topic in the catalog, find the category and book ID, then walk directly to the correct shelf.
That’s what indexes do in databases
. Instead of scanning the entire database (table), an index directs the system to the exact location of the data.

A database index is a data structure that allows quick retrieval of records from a table. Instead of scanning each row in a table, the index stores a reference (like a pointer) to the location of rows that match a certain condition.
Imagine an employee table with 1 million entries. A query like:

Without an index, the database checks every row — a full table scan. With an index on last_name, the system looks up "Smith" in the index, finds the matching references, and directly fetches the data — much faster.
CREATE INDEX idx_full_name ON employees(first_name, last_name);
Behind the scenes, indexes use optimized data structures (like B-Trees) that are sorted and searchable.

If users often search by price:
An index on price helps here:
Now, instead of comparing each row's price, the DB engine searches the idx_price index (sorted by price), finds the range, and jumps directly to relevant rows.
: Accelerates data retrieval from seconds to milliseconds
: Helps in fast ORDER BY queries

Imagine a flight booking system. Without indexes, finding all flights between Delhi and Mumbai requires checking every flight in the table. With an index on departure and destination, the system retrieves relevant entries instantly.

title: Types of Databases and When to Use Them

children: Databases are one of the foundational components of any system design. Whether you're building a small web app or designing a complex distributed system, choosing the right type of database plays a key role in performance, scalability, and maintainability.
In this article, we will explore
that are widely used in industry. We’ll break down how each works, when to use them, and look at real-world use cases and examples.

Relational databases structure data in tables consisting of rows and columns. Each table represents a specific entity, and rows correspond to individual records while columns define the attributes. Relationships between tables are established using keys (primary and foreign keys).
They provide strong consistency and support for complex queries and transactions using SQL. ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) ensure reliable processing.
E-commerce platforms handling user orders, inventory, and transactions

Key-Value stores are simple databases where data is stored as a collection of key-value pairs. Each key must be unique and directly maps to a single data value. They are highly performant and scale horizontally.
They offer minimal querying capabilities but are ideal for storing simple, unstructured data.
Document databases store data as documents (usually JSON, BSON, or XML). Each document is a self-contained unit that can include nested structures, making them suitable for semi-structured data.
They allow flexible schemas and dynamic data models which evolve over time.
Applications with frequently changing data structures

Graph databases store data in the form of nodes (entities), edges (relationships), and properties. They are optimized for traversing relationships and enable real-time querying across complex networks.
Wide-column stores manage data in tables, rows, and columns but allow each row to have different columns. This makes them efficient for sparse datasets and high write throughput scenarios.
They are designed for horizontal scaling and are schema-flexible.
In-memory databases store data in RAM instead of disk, delivering ultra-fast read and write performance. They are volatile and often used as a caching layer.
Time-series databases are optimized for time-stamped data points, typically collected at regular intervals. They offer efficient data ingestion, aggregation, and downsampling.
These databases store data as objects, consistent with object-oriented programming languages. Data and methods are encapsulated together, preserving object relationships.
Text search databases are built for indexing and querying large volumes of unstructured text. They offer features like full-text search, ranking, tokenization, and stemming.
Spatial databases manage geospatial data like coordinates, shapes, and locations. They provide spatial indexing, distance queries, and geometry functions.
Blob (Binary Large Object) datastores are optimized for storing unstructured binary data. They are used for storing media files and large documents.
Ledger databases are tamper-evident and provide immutable transaction logs. They are often used where auditability and transparency are crucial.
Hierarchical databases organize data in a tree-like structure with one-to-many relationships. While not commonly used today, they are foundational in mainframe environments.
Vector databases store high-dimensional vector embeddings used in machine learning and AI applications. They support fast similarity searches for nearest neighbor lookups.
Embedded databases run inside the host application as a library. They are lightweight and require minimal setup.

There is no one-size-fits-all database. The right choice depends on the structure of your data, scalability needs, consistency requirements, and access patterns. Understanding the trade-offs of each database type will help you design systems that are both efficient and scalable.

title: API Architecture: What is an API Gateway and Why It Matters

children: In the modern software landscape, APIs form the backbone of communication between different services. As applications scale and adopt microservice-based architectures, the number of APIs grows significantly. Managing this complexity requires a powerful pattern i.e. the

An API Gateway serves as the single entry point for client requests, simplifying how users and services interact with backend systems. It improves performance, enhances security, and centralizes critical responsibilities.
Let's dive deep into how API Gateways work, their importance, core features, and a real-world example to understand them in action.

An API Gateway is a server that acts as an intermediary between clients (such as web or mobile applications) and backend microservices. It receives incoming API requests, validates them, applies necessary logic (such as authentication or transformation), routes them to the correct service, and returns the response to the client.
Without an API Gateway, every client would need to communicate individually with multiple backend services, which would:
Make consistency and security harder to manage
With an API Gateway in place:
Clients send requests to a single endpoint
The Gateway handles security, traffic control, request routing, and more
Why Use an API Gateway? (Real-World Scenario)
Imagine a food delivery app like Swiggy or Zomato. When a user places an order, the system needs to:

Each of these steps might involve a separate backend service. Instead of the client interacting directly with all of them, the API Gateway receives the request and coordinates these services behind the scenes.
Core Features of an API Gateway
The Gateway verifies the identity of users (Authentication) and checks what they are allowed to do (Authorization).
Supports tokens like JWT or OAuth

How Does an API Gateway Work? (Step-by-Step with Example)
Let’s walk through the steps using a real-world scenario: placing a food delivery order.
The user taps "Place Order" in the app. The app sends a POST request with user ID, items, address, and payment method to the API Gateway.

is a situation where two or more processes cannot proceed because each is waiting for a resource that the other holds. This creates a cycle of dependencies with no process able to move forward.

Imagine two trains on a single track coming from opposite directions. Each train waits for the other to move, but neither can proceed unless the other backs up. Since both are waiting, no train moves. This is a real-life example of deadlock.

Another relatable example is two people trying to pass each other in a narrow hallway. If both move in the same direction at the same time and block each other's path, they may stay stuck, unless one steps aside.
In an operating system, a process typically:
A deadlock happens when multiple processes are holding resources and waiting to acquire resources held by each other.
Process 1 holds Resource A and wants Resource B.
Process 2 holds Resource B and wants Resource A.
Neither process can continue, and both are stuck in a deadlock.
A deadlock can occur only if all of the following four conditions are true:
: At least one resource must be non-shareable.
: A process holding one resource is waiting for additional resources.
: A resource cannot be forcibly taken away from a process holding it.
: A set of processes are each waiting for a resource that the next process in the cycle holds.
If any one of these conditions is eliminated, a deadlock cannot occur.
There are several strategies to handle deadlocks:
In this approach, the system is designed to prevent any of the four necessary conditions from holding.
: Use it only for truly non-shareable resources like printers.
: Ensure processes request all required resources at once.
: If a process waits, it must release its currently held resources.

This approach uses prior knowledge about future requests.
Before granting a resource request, the system simulates the allocation and checks if it leads to a safe state. If it does, the request is granted.
This ensures the system always stays in a safe state, avoiding deadlocks.
Deadlocks are allowed to occur, but the system must detect and resolve them.
If Process A is using a file and waiting for a printer, and Process B is using the printer and waiting for the file, one process must be terminated or its resource preempted to recover.
Used by systems like Windows and UNIX.
If they occur, restart the system

Deadlocks require four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

title: CPU Scheduling in Operating Systems

children: In the world of Operating Systems, understanding CPU scheduling is crucial to building efficient systems. CPU scheduling determines which process gets access to the CPU and when, directly affecting system performance, user experience, and resource utilization.
In this article, we’ll explore CPU Scheduling in depth, break down each scheduling algorithm, and explain their pros, cons, and real-world applications.

CPU Scheduling is the method by which the operating system selects a process from the ready queue to be executed by the CPU. Since the CPU can only execute one process at a time, scheduling helps in managing multiple processes by giving each process CPU time as efficiently as possible.
Why Do We Need CPU Scheduling?

Imagine running multiple apps on your phone. Only one app can actively use the CPU at a time. CPU scheduling decides which app runs when and for how long, making sure your system remains responsive and efficient.
Some processes may starve (never get CPU time)
CPU may remain idle if not properly utilized
Before diving into algorithms, here are a few key terms:
: When the process enters the ready queue.

The CPU can be taken away from a running process.
Example: A call interrupts your music app — the call gets CPU access.
Once the CPU is assigned, it cannot be taken away until the process finishes.
Example: Printer queue jobs where the first job prints fully before the next starts.
Let’s explore the main algorithms used for CPU scheduling with examples.
Processes are scheduled in the order they arrive.
Real World Example: Queue at a railway ticket counter.
Pros: Simple and easy to implement. Cons: High waiting time if a long job comes first (convoy effect).
The process with the smallest burst time is scheduled first.

Pros: Minimum average waiting time. Cons: Starvation of longer processes.
At any time, if a new process arrives with less remaining time, it preempts the current one.

Each process gets a fixed time slice (time quantum).
After time expires, the process goes to the back of the queue.

Pros: Fair and responsive. Cons: Performance depends heavily on time quantum.
Each process is assigned a priority. The CPU is assigned to the process with the highest priority.
Real World Example: Emergency services prioritized over regular appointments.
Pros: Important tasks are handled faster. Cons: Starvation of low-priority tasks.
Priority is based on response ratio = (Waiting Time + Burst Time) / Burst Time.
Real World Example: A restaurant prioritizing people who’ve been waiting long over new customers.
Pros: Balances short and long jobs fairly. Cons: Slightly complex.
Processes are divided into multiple queues based on priority or type (interactive, batch, etc).
Each queue has its own scheduling algorithm.
Real World Example: Airport lines for economy, business, and first-class passengers.
Pros: Efficient for diverse processes. Cons: Risk of starvation in lower queues.
Like MQS, but processes can move between queues based on their behavior.

Pros: Highly responsive and adaptive. Cons: Most complex to implement.

CPU scheduling is fundamental in multitasking systems. Each algorithm is designed for specific types of processes and use cases. Understanding them helps in designing faster, fairer, and more reliable systems.

title: Network Protocols

children: In the world of computer networks and system design, protocols play a vital role in ensuring communication between devices is smooth, secure, and reliable. Without protocols, it would be impossible for two computers or systems to exchange data effectively.
In this article, we will dive deep into what a protocol is and explore its various types with real-world examples to help you understand its importance in everyday networking and system design.

A protocol is a set of rules or standards that define how data is transmitted and received over a network. It governs everything from data formatting and transmission speed to error handling and security. Think of a protocol as a common language two computers agree to use to understand each other.

For example, when you visit a website, your browser uses a protocol called HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) to request and receive web pages from a server. Without HTTP, the communication between your browser and the server wouldn't make sense.
They standardize communication between different devices
Ensure data is transferred reliably and accurately
Enable interoperability between devices from different manufacturers
Protocols are categorized based on their function in a network. Below are the main types of protocols used in computer networks, explained in depth with real-world use cases.
These protocols define rules for data exchange between devices.
Used for: Accessing websites on the internet Example: When you type "
" in your browser, it uses HTTP to communicate with Google’s servers.
Used for: Secure communication over the web Example: Online banking websites use HTTPS to encrypt your transactions and personal data.
Used for: Transferring files between a client and server Example: A web developer uploads files to a website using an FTP client.
Used for: Sending emails Example: When you send an email through Gmail or Outlook, SMTP is used to deliver your message.
Used for: Receiving emails Example: POP3 downloads emails to your device, while IMAP syncs emails between your device and the server (e.g., accessing Gmail from phone and laptop).

title: Do you know what GPT means in ChatGPT?

blocks:
Do you know what GPT means in ChatGPT?

Generative Pre-trained Transformer, and it's easiest to understand backwards.

Transformer is the engine. Think of the rain forecast you saw as a kid: "70% chance of rain today." A transformer does the same thing with words, only far more advanced. Given everything so far, it scores every possible next token and gives each one a probability.

Pre-trained is how that engine learned. It was shown a huge amount of text from the internet and trained to predict the next word, billions of times over. After seeing "Sunday" followed by "Monday" enough times, ask it "what comes after Sunday?" and it says Monday with roughly 99% confidence.

Generative is what it does with those probabilities. It doesn't look up a stored answer. It samples one token, adds it to the input, and predicts again, building the reply word by word.

Two things I keep in mind every time I build with it.

It knows more than you, but it isn't smarter than you. It holds more data than any human brain can. Understanding context, making decisions and setting priorities are still on us. I don't see it as a replacement for people.

And it isn't deterministic. The same prompt can give a different answer, so "GPT said it" never means "it's correct." In production I treat its output like untrusted input: I validate it against a schema, check it against real data, and log it. Train it on garbage and you get confident garbage back.

#GenerativeAI #LLM #AIEngineering

title: One grey tick. Two grey ticks. Two blue ticks.

blocks:
One grey tick. Two grey ticks. Two blue ticks.

Three tiny icons on a chat app, and each one is a separate message travelling back to your phone.

Stripped down, the flow looks like this.

You hit send. Your phone pushes the message with an id it generated itself:

{"type":"msg","id":"3EB0A1","to":"user_42","body":"on my way"}

The server stores it and answers:

{"type":"ack","id":"3EB0A1","status":"sent"}

That's tick one. It only means the server has it. Your friend's phone could be switched off in a drawer.

When their phone comes online and pulls the message, it replies:

{"type":"receipt","id":"3EB0A1","status":"delivered"}

The server relays it to you. Tick two.

They open the chat, and one more goes out:

{"type":"receipt","id":"3EB0A1","status":"read"}

Blue.

The quiet hero here is that client-generated id. Mobile networks drop packets all day, so phones retry. The server dedupes on the id, which means a retry never becomes a duplicate message, and every receipt knows exactly which bubble to update.

It's the same idea I used to stop a pipeline from paying for the same LLM call twice: let the producer name the thing, and make every step idempotent on that name.

So when someone sits on two grey ticks for an hour, the server did its job. They just haven't opened it 😄

#SystemDesign #DistributedSystems #BackendEngineering

title: MCP sounds complicated until you see the actual message an agent sends.

blocks:
MCP sounds complicated until you see the actual message an agent sends.
It's about one line of JSON.

When an agent connects to an MCP server, the first thing it does is ask what tools exist:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/list"}

The server replies with each tool's name, a plain-English description, and a JSON Schema for its inputs:

{
"name": "get_order_status",
"description": "Get the current status of an order by its ID",
"inputSchema": {"type": "object",
"properties": {"order_id": {"type": "string"}},
"required": ["order_id"]}
}

That description is the part most people underestimate. The model never sees your code. It picks a tool purely by reading that one sentence, so a vague description means wrong tool calls no matter how good the model is.

Now a user asks "where's my order 4417?". The model decides this tool fits, and the client sends:

{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,"method":"tools/call",
 "params":{"name":"get_order_status","arguments":{"order_id":"4417"}}}

The server runs your function and sends the result back as content the model reads before it answers.

That's the whole loop: list, pick, call, read. It runs over stdio for local servers and over HTTP for remote ones.

What this changes about how I build MCP tools:

I write descriptions for the model, not for humans. I say when to use the tool and when not to.

I keep inputs small and typed. An enum beats a free-text string because the model can't invent a value that doesn't exist.

I return errors as readable text. "Order 4417 not found, check the ID" lets the agent recover. A raw 500 makes it guess.

Once you've seen the JSON, MCP stops being a buzzword. It's just an API contract that a model reads.

#AI #MCP #AIAgents

title: On 12 November, millions of people opened Outlook and nothing loaded.

blocks:
On 12 November, millions of people opened Outlook and nothing loaded.

Teams messages wouldn't send. Microsoft 365 apps kept spinning. Even some outside tools that connect to Microsoft stopped working. For some users it went on for more than 20 hours.

So what knocked out one of the biggest clouds in the world?

Not hackers, and not a sudden rush of users.

It started with a few servers that suddenly became unavailable.

Normally that's no big deal. If one server goes down, its traffic moves to the others. Think of a supermarket: when one counter closes, those customers join the other queues.

But this time, the other counters couldn't keep up.

The servers that were still running got all that extra traffic. They became overloaded, started failing too, and pushed even more traffic onto whatever was left.

One failure set off the next, and the next. 🧱🧱🧱

This is called a cascading failure.

Microsoft restarted servers and moved traffic around. But some servers came back up and went unresponsive again as soon as traffic returned. That's why the fix took so long.

The lesson for anyone building software:
- Redundancy means having enough backup capacity that losing a few servers doesn't sink the rest.
- Throttling means that when a server is overloaded, it accepts only what it can handle and politely says "try again later" to the rest, instead of slowing down for everyone and crashing.
- Fault tolerance means planning for "what if several things fail at once?"
- Recovery should be gradual. Bring traffic back slowly, not all at once.

If this can happen to Microsoft, it can happen to any system. Good engineering isn't about never failing. It's about stopping one failure from taking everything down.

Have you ever seen one small failure spread across a system? 👇

title: How does Blinkit get milk to your door in 10 minutes? 🛵

blocks:
How does Blinkit get milk to your door in 10 minutes? 🛵

It's not faster riders. It's system design.

Here's what happens in the few seconds after you tap "Order":

1️⃣ Your location picks the store
You're mapped to the nearest dark store, a small warehouse just 2–3 km away. The 10 minutes are decided before you even start browsing.

2️⃣ You only see what's really there
The catalog is filtered by that one store's live inventory, usually served from a cache like Redis so it loads instantly.

3️⃣ The last packet of milk problem
Two people order the last unit at the same moment. Without an atomic decrement or a row lock, both orders succeed and one customer gets a cancellation. Inventory reservation has to be race-proof.

4️⃣ Events, not waiting
The order goes onto a queue (think Kafka). The picker's app gets a pick list ordered by the store's layout, so packing takes about 2 minutes.

5️⃣ The rider is already there
Riders wait at the dark store. Assignment just picks the nearest free one, and GPS updates stream to your screen over WebSockets.

6️⃣ The real secret is overnight
Demand forecasting decides what each dark store stocks for tomorrow. Get that wrong and no amount of speed helps.

I work on backend systems for grocery retail, and the hardest part is never the happy path. It's inventory consistency at scale.

title: How does Twitter keep its Search system up and stable at massive scale?

blocks:
How does Twitter keep its Search system up and stable at massive scale?

Search sounds straightforward

User searches → Elasticsearch → results

But what happens when millions of tweets are created, traffic suddenly spikes, and you also need to ingest hundreds of terabytes of historical data?

I was going through Twitter’s architecture around Elasticsearch, and a few design decisions stood out.

### Why Elasticsearch?

It’s fast, distributed, horizontally scalable, and exposes simple REST APIs.

But there’s a problem.

### What happens when every team talks directly to Elasticsearch?

Who handles authentication?
Who enforces rate limits?
Who monitors cluster health?
What happens when one team sends too much traffic?

Twitter introduced an Elasticsearch proxy:

Client → Proxy → Elasticsearch

The proxy became a centralized layer for authentication, rate limiting, routing, monitoring, logging and cluster protection.

But that still leaves a bigger problem.

### What happens when traffic suddenly spikes?

Imagine a major event starts trending.

Millions of users start tweeting.

If every write goes directly to Elasticsearch, indexing latency shoots up and the cluster can become unstable.

### So what if we don't write to Elasticsearch immediately?

Twitter introduced an asynchronous path:

API → Proxy → Kafka → Workers → Elasticsearch

Kafka acts as a buffer.

If Elasticsearch slows down, workers can slow their consumption. If there’s a temporary failure, the events remain queued.

And there’s another advantage.

### What if we have thousands of individual indexing requests?

Workers can consume multiple events and make bulk indexing requests.

Fewer requests.
Better throughput.
Less pressure on Elasticsearch.

Now comes an even bigger challenge.

### What about massive backfills?

Real-time tweets are one thing.

But what if you need to ingest hundreds of terabytes of historical data?

You definitely don't want a huge MapReduce job directly hammering Elasticsearch.

So the architecture changes again:

MapReduce → HDFS/S3 → Workers → Elasticsearch

The backfill job first writes the data into distributed storage.

Then workers consume that data and gradually index it into Elasticsearch.

And now we can see the bigger pattern.

So what is the key idea?

Reads happen synchronously.

You need an answer to a search query, so the read goes to Elasticsearch.

Writes are deferred.

Instead of forcing Elasticsearch to handle every write immediately, you buffer, queue, batch and process them asynchronously.

And that’s the part I find most interesting about this architecture.

The system doesn’t try to make Elasticsearch handle everything. 

It changes the way work reaches Elasticsearch.

What’s your go-to move when the bottleneck isn’t slow enough, but simply getting too much work?

title: ☁️ We talk about AI as if it exists somewhere in the cloud

☁️ We talk about AI as if it exists somewhere in the cloud

But the cloud is not really a cloud.

It is thousands of buildings filled with servers, GPUs, networking equipment, storage, power infrastructure and cooling systems.

Data centers.

And while data centers are not new, the AI boom has completely changed the scale of what they need to support.

Think of a data center as a city built for computation, where servers do the work, racks house them, networking connects everything, storage holds the data, power keeps it running, and cooling keeps it from overheating.

When you open Instagram, make a UPI payment or send a request to ChatGPT, your request reaches physical infrastructure somewhere.

A server processes it, retrieves the required data and sends the response back.

Traditional applications rely heavily on CPUs.

AI workloads are different.

Training and serving large AI models requires massive parallel computation, making GPUs and specialized accelerators essential.

And more compute means:

→ More GPUs
→ More servers
→ More networking
→ More electricity
→ More heat
→ More cooling

Here's what people often miss:

AI data centers aren't constrained only by compute. Power and cooling are becoming critical challenges too.

A rack packed with AI accelerators can consume dramatically more power than traditional server racks.

So building an AI data center isn't simply about buying GPUs. You need the electrical infrastructure, networking, cooling and physical space to support them.

This is one reason liquid cooling is becoming increasingly relevant.

And networking has become critical too.

Modern AI training can involve thousands of accelerators working together, moving enormous amounts of data with very low latency.

Networking is no longer just about connecting servers. It has become part of the compute infrastructure itself.

The AI race isn't happening only at the model layer.

There's an entire physical stack underneath it:

Semiconductors → GPUs/AI accelerators → Servers → Networking → Data Centers → Power → Cooling

The model may be software.

But running it at global scale is very much a hardware and infrastructure problem.

So the next time someone says something is "in the cloud," picture a massive facility somewhere, with rows of machines working around the clock.

That's the cloud.

Just with a lot more electricity and cooling than the name suggests.

title: What actually happens in the few milliseconds after you hit “Google Search”?

blocks:
What actually happens in the few milliseconds after you hit “Google Search”? 

You type:

best restaurants near me

Hit Enter.

And almost instantly, Google gives you thousands or millions of results.

But there are hundreds of billions of webpages and other content in Google's Search index.

So is Google searching through all of them from scratch every time you make a query?

No.

The interesting part is that Google does a huge amount of the work before you even search.

First, Google crawls the web and discovers pages.

Then it processes them and adds information about them to its Search index.

Think of it like the index at the back of a massive book.

Instead of searching every page for:

database

a search engine can maintain an index that conceptually looks like:

database → Page A, Page B, Page C...

This is the basic idea behind an inverted index.

Now when you search:

database system design

the system can quickly retrieve pages associated with those terms instead of starting from the entire web.

But finding matching pages is only the beginning.

Google then has to figure out:

Which results are actually useful for this query?

Its ranking systems consider many signals, including the meaning of your query, relevance, content quality, usability, freshness, language, location and more.

And there can be thousands or even millions of potential matches.

So the search infrastructure has to process these enormous indexes efficiently and return useful results in a fraction of a second.

A simplified view looks like:

Crawl → Index → Retrieve → Rank → Serve

And here's the part I find most interesting:

Google isn't “searching the internet” from scratch when you hit Search.

A huge amount of the work happened before you ever typed your query.

The query-time work is closer to:

Understand → Retrieve → Rank → Return

And Google says its systems are specifically optimized to reduce latency, with teams working to shave milliseconds off different parts of Search.

That's one of the fundamental ideas behind building systems at massive scale:

Do the expensive work beforehand, so the user doesn't have to wait for it.

title: The Genius Behind Instagram’s “Infinite Scroll” 👀

blocks:
The Genius Behind Instagram’s “Infinite Scroll” 👀

You keep scrolling.

And scrolling.

And somehow, there’s always another Reel ready for you.

That’s what makes infinite scroll feel so effortless. You don’t have to wait for the next piece of content. You just keep going.

Read till the end for one interesting fact 👀

So let’s break down how this works.

First, the recommendation algorithm tries to predict what you’re likely to watch next.

It can use signals like:

→ What you’ve watched before
→ What you’ve liked, shared, or saved
→ How long you watched a Reel
→ What you tend to skip
→ What similar users are engaging with

Based on these signals, it can rank a bunch of Reels and decide which ones are most relevant to you.

And then comes the interesting part.

The app can prefetch parts of the likely next Reel while you’re still watching the current one.
A simplified flow looks something like:

Recommendation → Prefetch → CDN → Local buffer → Play

Instead of waiting for you to swipe and then downloading the video, the app can start fetching it in advance from a nearby CDN.

The video is delivered in smaller chunks, so while you’re watching the current Reel, the next one can already be getting downloaded in the background.

So when you swipe:

→ The video is already partially downloaded
→ The player already has data in its buffer
→ Playback can start almost immediately
But there’s another interesting problem.

What if Instagram preloads a Reel you never watch?

Doing this for every possible Reel would waste a huge amount of bandwidth.

So the system has to balance:

Relevance vs. playback speed vs. bandwidth vs. battery

And then there’s adaptive bitrate streaming, which can adjust the video quality based on your network conditions.

So that tiny swipe that feels instantaneous?

Behind it, you have:

• Recommendation algorithms
• Prefetching
• CDNs
• Caching
• Video chunking
• Adaptive bitrate streaming
• Bandwidth optimization

Simple to use.

Not so simple to build.

And if you really read till the end, here’s the interesting fact 👀

Instagram doesn’t need to download the entire Reel before you can start watching it.

It can load enough of the video into your buffer to start playback, while the rest continues downloading in the background.

So by the time you swipe, the video feels like it was already waiting for you.

And that’s how the infinite scroll keeps rolling.

title: iPhone 17 at ₹50K during Big Billion Days 👀

blocks:
iPhone 17 at ₹50K during Big Billion Days 👀


Haha, hold on. Forget the ₹50K for a second 😂

Let’s say you open the app, see “Only 5 left”, and hit Buy Now.

So do 10,000 other people.

Now the interesting question:

How does the backend decide who actually gets those 5 iPhones?

It’s not as simple as:

→ Check inventory
→ If stock > 0, place the order
→ Reduce stock

Because thousands of requests can reach the backend almost at the same time.

Two requests could read:

stock = 1

before either one updates it.

And suddenly, the same iPhone could be sold twice 😬

So the system needs to make the inventory update atomic.

For example:

UPDATE inventory SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE product_id = X AND stock > 0

If the update succeeds:

→ Inventory reserved
→ Continue with the order

If it affects 0 rows:

→ Someone else got it
→ Sorry, better luck next time 🥲

But inventory is only the beginning.

What if the payment succeeds but the order request times out?

What if the user clicks Pay twice?

What if the payment fails after the inventory was reserved?

Now you need to think about:

title: Sometimes, the fastest database query is the one you never execute.

paragraph:
Sometimes, the fastest database query is the one you never execute.

That's the basic idea behind Bloom Filters.

Before performing an expensive lookup, a Bloom Filter helps answer a simple question:

Could this key exist?

The answer can be:

Definitely not
or
Probably yes

If it's definitely not present, we can skip the lookup.

If it's probably present, we perform the actual lookup.

The interesting part is that Bloom Filters don't store the actual data.

They use a bit array and multiple hash functions to keep just enough information to determine whether an element could exist.

This makes them extremely memory efficient.

But there is a trade-off.

Bloom Filters can have false positives, but they can never have false negatives.

This simple idea is useful in systems such as Cassandra, Bigtable, HBase, Redis, and other large-scale systems where avoiding unnecessary disk or database reads can make a significant difference.

title: HTTP just got its first new standardized request method in more than 20 years.

paragraph:
HTTP just got its first new standardized request method in more than 20 years.

It's called QUERY.

At first, it might seem like just another HTTP method. But it actually solves a problem that many backend engineers have encountered while designing APIs.

Suppose you're building a product search endpoint where users can filter by:

• Multiple brands
• Price range
• Categories
• Rating
• Availability
• Sorting options

Traditionally, we'd use a GET request.

http
GET /products?brands=Apple,Samsung&minPrice=30000&maxPrice=80000&rating=4...

This works well for simple queries, but as more filters are added, the URL quickly becomes long, difficult to read, and harder to maintain. It can also run into URL length limitations imposed by browsers, proxies, or servers.

To avoid this, many APIs use POST instead and send the filters as a JSON request body.

{
 "brands": ["Apple", "Samsung"],
 "price": {
  "min": 30000,
  "max": 80000
 },
 "rating": 4,
 "inStock": true
}

While this makes the request much cleaner, there's one issue.

A search operation doesn't create or modify anything. It's simply asking the server to return data. Using POST works technically, but it doesn't accurately describe the intent of the request.

That's where QUERY comes in.

It allows clients to send a request body while explicitly indicating that the operation is read-only.

In other words:

• You get the flexibility of a request body.
• The request still represents a read operation.
• API semantics become clearer and more consistent.

This may seem like a small addition, but it's significant because it's the first new standardized HTTP request method in more than two decades.

Even technologies that have been around for decades continue to evolve as new engineering challenges emerge.

Everyone talks about AI hallucinations and bias

But there’s a quieter problem that might be more dangerous.

👉 AI that agrees with you too much.

Both OpenAI and Anthropic have acknowledged this as a major issue.

AI systems tend to validate your opinions, even when you’re wrong.

And it’s not random.

A study by Stanford University found that top models like GPT, Claude, and Gemini are ~49% more likely to agree with users than humans are.

So why does this happen?

There are two layers to it:

1. Technical reason (RLHF)
Most modern AI models are trained using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback.

Humans rate responses.
AI learns what gets higher ratings.

And guess what humans tend to reward?

✔️ Agreement
✔️ Validation
✔️ “You’re right” energy

So the model optimizes for that.

2. Psychological + business reason

Let’s be honest.

A system that agrees with you feels:
• Smarter
• Friendlier
• Easier to trust

It becomes… addictive.

And more engagement = more usage = more growth.

So naturally, a “yes-man AI” performs better as a product.

Now the real question:

Are we building AI that challenges humans to think better
or AI that simply keeps humans comfortable?

title: Do you know the difference between AI Agents and Agentic AI?

blocks:
Do you know the difference between AI Agents and Agentic AI?

A lot of people use these terms interchangeably.
But they’re fundamentally different.

Let’s break it down with a practical example 👇

Imagine you’re building a system for trip planning.

A user says:
"I want to plan a 3-day trip to Goa within ₹15,000."

👉 What an AI Agent does:

An AI agent handles a specific task.

For example:

One agent finds flights
One agent suggests hotels
One agent lists places to visit

Each agent executes its job.
But you still decide how everything fits together.

👉 What a Multi-Agent System does:

Now multiple agents work together:

Travel agent (flights/trains)
Accommodation agent
Itinerary agent

They collaborate and give a combined output.

Better. But still predefined coordination.

👉 What Agentic AI does:

This is where the shift happens.

Same input:
"3-day Goa trip under ₹15,000"

Now the system:
 • Understands constraints (budget, duration, preferences)
 • Creates a plan (travel + stay + activities allocation)
 • Decides trade-offs (cheap flight vs better hotel)
 • Chooses which tools/agents to use
 • Executes in the right sequence
 • Adapts if something fails (e.g., budget exceeded → replan)

It doesn’t just execute tasks.
It thinks, plans, and orchestrates like a human would.

The core difference:
 • AI Agents → Do tasks
 • Multi-Agent Systems → Do multiple tasks together
 • Agentic AI → Decides what tasks to do, how to do them, and in what order

Not every problem needs Agentic AI.

But when it does,
it changes everything.

From executing tasks
to actually figuring out what needs to be done.

title: What happens when you upload a file to Amazon S3?

blocks:
What happens when you upload a file to Amazon S3?

Let’s understand it step by step 👇

At a high level, S3 works with two core layers:

• Bucket (metadata layer)
• Object (data + metadata)

Now here’s the actual flow:

1. You create a bucket
The bucket is not where your file physically lives
It exists in the metadata layer and acts as a logical container
It defines namespace, region, policies, and access control

2. Client sends a PUT request
When you upload a file, Your application sends an HTTP PUT request to S3 (often signed using AWS Signature V4)

3. S3 checks:
– Does the bucket exist?
– Do you have permission to upload?
– It validates:
  IAM policies / bucket policies
 ACLs (if used)
 Request signature

4. Request is routed internally
S3 routes the request to the appropriate partition based on the object key (This is part of how S3 achieves horizontal scaling)

5. Metadata is prepared
Before storing the file, S3 creates metadata like:
– Key (object name)
– Size, content-type
– Timestamps, storage class
– Version ID (if versioning is enabled)

6. Data gets stored
The object data is written to multiple storage nodes across Availability Zones
S3 ensures high durability (11 9’s) by replicating the data

7. Unique Object ID is generated
S3 assigns an ID that links your file’s data with its metadata
It is an internal identifier that maps the object’s data to its metadata
S3 provides strong read-after-write consistency for PUT operations

8. Metadata store is updated
The metadata layer is updated with object location, version, and attributes
This enables fast lookup and retrieval

S3 is not just a storage service
It’s a distributed system that separates compute, metadata, and storage layers

That’s why it works reliably even at massive scale!

title: Dead Letter Queues are one of those small concepts that quietly save production systems.

blocks:
Dead Letter Queues are one of those small concepts that quietly save production systems.

When a message fails to be processed
Maybe the data is malformed
Maybe a downstream service is down

What do you do?
Drop it? Retry forever?

Neither.

You send it to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ).

A DLQ is a separate queue for messages that fail after a defined number of retries.
They don’t block your main flow. They don’t keep consuming resources. They wait until someone inspects and fixes them.

Without DLQs
• One bad message can block the entire queue
• Continuous retries can waste resources

With DLQs
• The main system keeps running
• Failures are isolated and easier to debug

Any async system at scale should include a DLQ.

Would love to know how others handle failed messages in their systems.

title: Your service is slow… but CPU usage is low. What do you check first?

blocks:
Your service is slow… but CPU usage is low. What do you check first?

It feels counterintuitive.

If CPU isn’t busy, why is the system slow?

Because most performance issues aren’t about doing too much work…
they’re about waiting too long.

Here’s how I approach it:

1. Thread / Process State
 • Are workers blocked on locks?
 • Waiting on I/O?
 • Stuck in queues?
If your system isn’t using CPU, chances are it’s idle… but not by choice.

2. External Dependencies
 • Database latency
 • Third-party APIs
 • Internal microservices
A slow dependency can quietly drag your entire system down.

3. Database Bottlenecks
 • Missing indexes
 • Inefficient queries
 • Connection pool limits
Databases are often the hidden gravity well of latency.

4. Lock Contention
 • Shared resources causing blocking
 • Poor concurrency design
Low CPU + high latency often points to threads waiting their turn.

5. I/O Wait
 • Disk reads/writes
 • Network delays
 • Logging overhead
I/O is the silent saboteur. It slows everything without spiking CPU.

6. Queue Backlogs
 • Message queues piling up
 • Thread pools saturated
 • Requests waiting before execution
Sometimes the system isn’t slow… it’s just not getting to work yet.

7. Resource Limits (Other than CPU)
 • Memory pressure
 • File descriptors
 • Network bandwidth
CPU is just one piece of the puzzle.

If CPU usage is low, your system isn’t overloaded… it’s waiting somewhere. And the real skill is figuring out where that wait begins.
