title: How do you deploy 20+ microservices with zero downtime?

blocks:
How do you deploy 20+ microservices with zero downtime?

When systems scale, deployments can’t afford disruption. A single failed release can impact thousands of users in seconds.

Here are some key strategies that make seamless deployments possible:

✔ Blue-Green Deployment
Maintain two identical environments: Blue (live) and Green (new version).
 • Deploy the new version to the Green environment
 • Run validations and health checks
 • Switch traffic from Blue to Green once stable
This approach allows instant rollback by redirecting traffic back if needed.

✔ Canary Release
Roll out changes incrementally to a small subset of users:
 • Start with a small percentage (e.g., 1–5%)
 • Monitor system metrics like errors, latency, and usage patterns
 • Gradually increase traffic if everything performs as expected
This helps limit the impact of potential issues.

✔ Kubernetes Rolling Updates
In containerized environments, Kubernetes manages deployments efficiently:
 • New instances (pods) are created alongside existing ones
 • Traffic is gradually shifted to the new version
 • Old instances are terminated only after stability is confirmed
This ensures continuous availability during updates.

✔ Feature Flags
Decouple deployment from feature release:
 • Deploy code without immediately exposing new functionality
 • Enable features selectively for users or regions
 • Disable features instantly without redeploying
This provides fine-grained control and safer experimentation.

In practice, these strategies are often combined to achieve both reliability and speed.
For example, using feature flags alongside canary releases and rolling updates enables controlled, observable, and reversible deployments.

The objective is not just to deploy faster, but to deploy safely, predictably, and without disrupting users.

title: An API responds in ~100ms for users in the US, but takes ~2 seconds for users in India.

blocks:
An API responds in ~100ms for users in the US, but takes ~2 seconds for users in India.

At first glance, it looks like a backend bug.
In reality, it’s a standard system design problem.

When users are far from your servers, latency increases due to network distance, routing, and multiple hops. Optimizing code alone won’t fix this.

What actually works is designing systems for global scale:

1. Region-based deployments
Serve users from the nearest geographic region instead of a single centralized server.

2. Content Delivery Network (CDN)
Cache static and frequently accessed data closer to users to reduce backend dependency.

3. Caching layer (Redis / API Gateway)
Minimize repeated database calls and reduce response time.

4. Database replication
Route read operations to the nearest replica while keeping writes controlled.

5. Geo-routing
Automatically direct users to the closest available server.

6. API optimization
Reduce payload size, enable compression, and use efficient protocols like HTTP/2.

What seems like a performance issue in code is often a distribution problem in architecture.

This is what real-world system design looks like.

title: 𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗣𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗻’𝘀 𝗚𝗮𝗿𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺𝘀?

blocks:
𝗗𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗣𝘆𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗻’𝘀 𝗚𝗮𝗿𝗯𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗺𝗲𝗺𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺𝘀?

For a long time, I had this assumption:
Python handles memory automatically, so I don’t really need to think about it.

But recently, while exploring this deeper, I realized something important.

Python does manage memory automatically, but automatic doesn’t mean foolproof.

Python primarily uses reference counting, where every object keeps track of how many references point to it. When this count drops to zero, the memory is freed immediately.

Along with this, Python also uses a garbage collector to handle more complex cases like circular references.

So at a high level, it feels like everything is taken care of.

But in practice, things are a bit different.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸𝘆
What I found interesting is that Python doesn’t free memory based on whether you need an object.
It frees memory only when there are no references left.

Which means:

You can stop using an object…
but if something still references it, it stays in memory.

Relatable scenarios most of us encounter:

1. Caching and global data
You store data in a global variable or cache “just in case.”
It keeps growing quietly and never gets released.

2. Circular references
Two objects referencing each other can prevent memory from being freed because their reference count never reaches zero.

3. Long-running applications
In scripts, you may never notice.
But in servers or background jobs, small memory retention keeps adding up over time.

4. Resources not explicitly closed
Files, DB connections, sockets - they may stay open longer than expected if not handled properly.

Realization - Garbage Collection in Python is powerful, but it works based on reachability, not usefulness.

It cannot decide whether your object is still logically needed.
It only checks if something still points to it.

Earlier, I thought memory management in Python was something I could ignore.

Now I see it differently.

You don’t need to manage memory manually,
but you definitely need to understand how it behaves.

Because most memory issues don’t fail immediately.
They show up later, when your system scales.

title: 🚩 Red Flag: Blocking users by IP

blocks:
🚩 Red Flag: Blocking users by IP

A common reaction to API abuse is to block the attacker’s IP address.
However, this can unintentionally block many legitimate users.

In many environments like corporate offices, universities, or campuses, thousands of users share the same public IP due to NAT (Network Address Translation). Blocking that IP can therefore deny access to an entire organization.

Better approach:
• Prefer rate limiting by User_ID or API_Key whenever authentication exists.
• Use IP-based limits only for unauthenticated endpoints.
• Apply higher thresholds for IP limits to reduce false positives.
• Consider combining IP + user-level limits for better protection.

IP addresses often represent networks, not individual users, so relying solely on IP blocking can lead to unintended service disruptions.

𝗠𝘆 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗸𝘀 (𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗜𝘁’𝘀 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗝𝘂𝘀𝘁 “𝗕𝗶𝗴 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮”)

Recently, I worked on Databricks as part of a data workflow implementation and spent time exploring its architecture in depth. My initial understanding was that it was primarily a managed Spark platform. That’s technically correct.

However, after working with it hands-on, I realized it represents a broader architectural approach to modern data systems.

𝗟𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗵𝗼𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲
Databricks is built around the Lakehouse model, combining scalable object storage with warehouse-level reliability.

With Delta Lake, it introduces:
 • ACID transactions on cloud object storage
 • Schema enforcement and schema evolution
 • Time travel through versioned transaction logs
 • Optimistic concurrency control

The presence of a transaction log layer fundamentally changes the behavior of data stored in object storage. Instead of treating files as static blobs, Delta maintains metadata and commit logs that enable snapshot isolation and consistent reads across distributed workloads.

𝗦𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗲
The strict separation between storage and compute is another strong architectural decision.

Clusters can scale independently. Compute resources can be tuned per workload. Storage remains durable and decoupled. From a system design perspective, this improves elasticity and fault isolation while keeping infrastructure flexible.

𝗨𝗻𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗲𝗱 𝗕𝗮𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴
Databricks leverages Spark’s structured APIs to unify batch and streaming processing.

Streaming workloads are treated as incremental structured queries, which simplifies pipeline design. Instead of maintaining separate architectures for real-time and historical data, both follow a consistent processing model built on execution DAGs and distributed task scheduling.

𝗚𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
Unity Catalog introduces centralized governance:
 • Fine-grained access control
 • Data lineage tracking
 • Cross-workspace metadata management

This effectively creates a control plane over distributed data assets, which becomes critical as systems scale.

𝗠𝘆 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲
Coming from a backend engineering background, what I found particularly interesting was how closely Databricks reflects core distributed systems concepts:
 • Transaction logs managing distributed state
 • Snapshot isolation across object storage
 • DAG-based execution planning
 • Lazy evaluation and query optimization
 • Partition pruning and file-level indexing
 • Fault tolerance via lineage-based recomputation

Understanding these internals makes it particularly interesting from a backend and system design perspective, especially when thinking in terms of distributed state management, execution planning, and concurrency control.

If you use RabbitMQ, once a worker reads a message, it gets deleted.
It’s a queue.

If you use Kafka, the message stays there.
It’s an append-only log.

In practice:
If you need multiple different microservices to react to the exact same event independently (and potentially replay past events), you need an Event Stream, not a standard Message Queue

title: In a monolith, transactions are easy.

paragraph:
In a monolith, transactions are easy.
Everything runs inside a single database transaction. If one step fails, the entire operation rolls back.

Microservices don’t work that way.
Each service owns its own database, network calls can fail, and locking multiple databases in a single transaction isn’t practical. That’s where the Saga Design Pattern becomes useful.

paragraph:
OpenAI recently released an article on 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗦𝗤𝗟 𝘁𝗼 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝟴𝟬𝟬 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗚𝗣𝗧 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀.

After reading it, here are my key takeaways.

Despite a 10x growth in database load over the past year, OpenAI still runs a 𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲-𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘆 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗦𝗤𝗟 𝘀𝗲𝘁𝘂𝗽 with nearly 𝟱𝟬 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘀 distributed globally. Instead of premature sharding, the focus was on disciplined optimization, vertical scaling, and offloading read-heavy traffic to replicas.

The real challenge was write scalability.  Due to 𝗣𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗴𝗿𝗲𝗦𝗤𝗟’𝘀 𝗠𝗩𝗖𝗖 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹, write-heavy workloads caused amplification and operational overhead. To address this, shardable write-heavy workloads were migrated to systems like Azure Cosmos DB, while PostgreSQL remained unsharded to avoid large-scale application changes.

What stood out most was the engineering pragmatism. Fixing redundant writes, introducing lazy writes, auditing expensive ORM-generated queries, using PgBouncer for connection pooling, isolating workloads, and protecting the database from cache-miss spikes all played a key role.

A great reminder that scaling is often about strong fundamentals, not exotic systems.

Shoutout to Bohan Zhang from OpenAI for a clear and insightful write-up.

title: Recently I’ve been working with Elasticsearch, and it’s been a great learning experience.

blocks:
Recently I’ve been working with Elasticsearch, and it’s been a great learning experience.

What stood out to me is how thoughtfully its architecture is designed for scale and performance.

Instead of relying on a single database instance, Elasticsearch distributes data across multiple nodes. Each index is broken into shards, and those shards are replicated across the cluster. This allows queries to be processed in parallel, which is a big reason why search and analytics remain fast even as data grows.

Another important aspect is how Elasticsearch handles indexing. Data is stored in a structure optimized for retrieval, making full-text search, filtering, and aggregations highly efficient. From a backend perspective, this changes how you think about designing APIs and building data-heavy features.

I’ve only started exploring its capabilities, but it has already given me better insight into building scalable and responsive systems.
In the future, I’ll definitely be writing a detailed article on Elasticsearch and its real-world use cases.

title: While working on distributed systems, I finally started appreciating the real meaning of the CAP Theorem.

blocks:
While working on distributed systems, I finally started appreciating the real meaning of the CAP Theorem.

In theory, we learn that a system can only guarantee two out of:
 • Consistency
 • Availability
 • Partition Tolerance

But when you’re designing real services, this isn’t an abstract concept.
It shows up in very practical decisions:
• Do we serve slightly stale data or fail the request?
• Do we block writes during a network partition or allow divergence?
• Do we optimize for uptime or for strict correctness in this workflow?

For example, when network partitions happen (and they always do at scale), the system must choose:
CP: Preserve correctness, possibly rejecting some requests
AP: Remain responsive, even if data becomes temporarily inconsistent

There is no universally “right” choice.
The correct decision depends on the business requirement, the user experience you want to protect, and the type of data being handled.

Working on real distributed systems taught me that CAP is not just a theorem.
It’s a design conversation you have every time you build something that needs to scale reliably.

title: 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗲𝗯𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗗𝗼 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸?

blocks:
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗪𝗲𝗯𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗗𝗼 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸?

In today’s highly connected digital world, no system truly works alone.
E-commerce platforms talk to payment gateways, payment gateways talk to banks, and banks update customer accounts.
This constant, real-time communication is what powers modern applications.

One of the most common ways systems communicate is through webhooks.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝘄𝗲𝗯𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸?
A webhook is an HTTP request triggered automatically by an event in one system and sent to another system with event data.

In short:
Event happens → webhook fires → another system reacts.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗯𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿?
Webhooks notify one system when something important happens in another.

For example:
When your credit card is charged for a subscription, the banking system sends a webhook to the service, which then sends you an email notification.
No polling. No waiting. Just real-time updates.

They are a core building block of event-driven applications and architectures.

𝗪𝗲𝗯𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸 𝘃𝘀 𝗔𝗣𝗜
APIs are for requesting actions or data.
Webhooks are for receiving notifications when actions happen.

Both work together.
APIs create events.
Webhooks respond to them.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘄𝗲𝗯𝗵𝗼𝗼𝗸𝘀 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸
 1. You register a public endpoint URL with a provider (Stripe, GitHub, Twilio, etc.).
 2. You subscribe to specific events like payment.created or user.updated.
 3. When the event occurs, the provider sends an HTTP request to your endpoint.
 4. Your system processes the event.

Key things to handle in real systems
 • At-least-once delivery → make your processing idempotent
 • Short timeouts → acknowledge fast, process asynchronously
 • High traffic bursts → use queues
 • Out-of-order events → rely on timestamps
 • Security risks → always verify webhook signatures (HMAC)

Webhooks look simple, but in production they require serious engineering discipline.
Used correctly, they enable scalable, reliable, real-time systems.

For anyone working on backend systems, developing a good understanding of webhooks can be very helpful.

title: 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝗳 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗺𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗳𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲?

blocks:
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝗶𝗳 𝘁𝘄𝗼 𝗺𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗶𝗳𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲?

A friend recently asked me this question, and after exploring it, here are the key findings. In this post, I will try to cover it in brief so that everyone can understand.

When two independent services attempt to write to the same data, the system can run into issues like lost updates, version conflicts, and inconsistent state. To handle this, backend systems generally follow a few well-established approaches:

1. Pessimistic Locking
The database locks the record during a transaction to prevent parallel writes. Reliable, but may affect performance.

2. Optimistic Locking
Each record has a version or timestamp, and updates succeed only if versions match. This scales well and is widely used.

3. Distributed Locking
Using tools like Redis or ZooKeeper when multiple services across nodes need exclusive access.

4. Event or Saga-Based Designs
Instead of writing directly to the same table, services communicate through events and avoid touching the same record.

Most importantly:
Each microservice should ideally own its data. If two services need interaction on the same business entity, sharing information through events or APIs is safer than competing writes to a shared table.

title: 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝘆𝘀 “𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗹𝗼𝘄”

blocks:
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗜 𝗻𝗼𝘄 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝘆𝘀 “𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗹𝗼𝘄”

When I started working on backend systems, I used to jump straight into the code.
Over time, I learned that slowness is rarely a code problem. It’s about where the time is going.

So before touching the implementation, this is the checklist I follow:

𝟭. 𝗜𝘀 𝗶𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗼𝗿 𝗯𝗮𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗻𝗱?
 • Check TTFB vs total response time
 • Slow before first byte = backend
 • Slow after = client / network / payload size
Many “slow APIs” are actually slow clients.

𝟮. 𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗱𝗲𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆?
Break the request into parts:
 • Auth / middleware
 • Database
 • Cache
 • External APIs
 • Background jobs accidentally running inline
One slow dependency = slow API.

𝟯. 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁, 𝗮𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗔𝘀𝗸:
 • Is this query indexed?
 • Is it doing more work than needed?
 • N+1 queries?
 • Full collection scan hiding behind small data?
Most backend slowness lives here.

𝟰. 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗲 𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗲 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱𝗻’𝘁?
Common mistakes:
 • Calling external services synchronously
 • Heavy computation inside the request cycle
 • Waiting for background tasks to finish
Async APIs with sync work are still slow.

𝟱. 𝗖𝗼𝗹𝗱 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗿𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱
Check for:
 • Lambda or container cold starts
 • New DB connections per request
 • DNS or TLS setup on every call
These don’t show up in code reviews but hurt latency.

𝟲. 𝗥𝗲𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀, 𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲𝗼𝘂𝘁𝘀, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗳𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀
 • Is the request retrying under the hood?
 • Are timeouts too high?
 • Is one failed dependency stalling everything?
Retries without limits create hidden latency.

𝟳. 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱 𝘀𝗶𝘇𝗲
 • Over-fetching data
 • Large JSON responses
 • Uncompressed responses
Latency isn’t only compute. Bytes matter.

𝟴. 𝗟𝗼𝗴𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀
Check:
 • Request duration breakdowns
 • Slow request logs
 • P95 and P99, not averages
Averages lie. Tail latency is what users feel.

Slow APIs are rarely fixed by faster code. They’re fixed by understanding where the time is actually spent.

title: 𝗔𝘀𝘆𝗻𝗰 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿!

blocks:
𝗔𝘀𝘆𝗻𝗰 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿!

It means non-blocking, not lower latency.

I’ve seen systems marked “async” still feel slow because the bottleneck never moved.
The API was async.
The database was still slow.
The external service still took 800ms.

Async helps when you are:
• Waiting on I/O
• Calling external services
• Handling concurrency at scale

It does nothing for:
• Heavy CPU work
• Poor queries
• Bad system design

Async improves 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝗽𝘂𝘁, not 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆.

If one request takes 1 second, async won’t make it 100 ms.
It just allows the system to do other work while waiting.

Real performance gains come from better queries, caching, batching, and fewer network hops.
Async improves scalability, not the fundamental cost of work.

title: I recently built a microservice from scratch, and while working through the implementation, I focused on identifying the essential best practices that actually make development and maintenance easier in the long run.

blocks:
I recently built a microservice from scratch, and while working through the implementation, I focused on identifying the essential best practices that actually make development and maintenance easier in the long run. 

These are not theoretical ideals. They’re practical, must-do choices that directly boost productivity later when the system grows or requirements change.

𝟭. 𝗞𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗲𝗮𝗰𝗵 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗮𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗺𝗼𝘂𝘀
A microservice should have its own data, logic, and lifecycle. This avoids cross-service dependencies that slow down development and make debugging harder. Autonomy directly translates to faster iteration.

𝟮. 𝗗𝗲𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗯𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗰𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆
Clear API contracts prevent confusion. When request and response formats are predictable, every integration becomes smoother. This is one of the simplest ways to reduce friction across teams.

𝟯. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗱𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝗻𝗲
Timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers are not “optimizations.” They’re the foundation of a stable distributed system. Adding them early prevents a lot of operational pain later.

𝟰. 𝗨𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝘆𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗽𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗮𝘁𝗲
Message queues and event-driven flows help decouple services. This reduces bottlenecks, improves performance, and makes the system more adaptable without rewriting core logic.

𝟱. 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗼𝗯𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆
Good logs, metrics, and tracing give you a clear view of what’s happening inside the system. When an issue appears, you solve it faster because the service already tells you where to look.

𝟲. 𝗗𝗲𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆 𝗶𝗻 𝘀𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗹, 𝘀𝗮𝗳𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗽𝘀
Smaller releases reduce risk and make rollbacks straightforward. This habit alone can save an entire team from long debugging cycles during production incidents.

𝟳. 𝗧𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁-𝗶𝗻 𝗿𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁
Input validation, authentication, authorization, and rate-limiting shouldn’t be afterthoughts. Adding them early protects both the system and the development velocity.

These practices aren’t dramatic or complex, but they compound over time. Setting them up early makes the system easier to scale, easier to maintain, and much more predictable to work with.

If you're building microservices or planning to adopt them, these principles form a solid baseline that pays off in productivity as the architecture evolves.

title: 𝗚𝗣𝗨𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗔𝗜 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗮𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗱!

blocks:
𝗚𝗣𝗨𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗔𝗜 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗮𝗹𝗴𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗵𝗺 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗱!

Neural networks existed in the 1980s.
Backpropagation existed.
Even large datasets existed.

Yet AI only exploded recently.

Why?

Because CPUs think in sequence.
GPUs think in parallel.

And modern AI is nothing but:
Millions of matrix calculations
Happening at the same time.

Originally, GPUs were built for one job:
Rendering pixels in video games 

Today, they train models with
Billions of parameters 

Same math.
Different universe.

Algorithms gave AI intelligence.
GPUs gave AI speed.
And speed is what unlocked scale.

From:
Training a single model in months
To:
Training thousands in days

AI didn’t suddenly become smart.
It finally became 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗲𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿.

title: 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗟𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗵?

blocks:
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗟𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲 𝗟𝗮𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝗵?

I have heard this question many times and even noticed it myself.

LLMs are great at writing, but the moment you give them a slightly tricky math problem, they can get confused.
So I looked into it, and here’s what I found.

LLMs don’t actually calculate. They predict the next word based on patterns.
Math is not about patterns. It’s about exact rules.
So the model often gives an answer that looks right instead of doing the real calculation.

Even when we ask it to show the steps, those steps are just text it has learned from examples.
They are not guaranteed to be logical or correct, and one small mistake throws everything off.

Numbers also behave differently from normal words, and the model doesn’t fully understand that small changes in numbers can completely change the result.

Researchers are working on this by combining LLMs with proper math engines and adding checks before the final answer is given.

𝗙𝘂𝗻 𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁: Even the most advanced LLMs sometimes get basic multiplication wrong, but they can explain quantum mechanics perfectly.

title: 𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗴𝗼 𝗯𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀?

blocks:
𝗦𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗴𝗼 𝗯𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀?

I have been thinking a lot about this tradeoff lately. Relational systems like MySQL and PostgreSQL have powered our applications for decades. They are stable, mature, and easy to work with. But as data grows more complex and applications scale differently, it is worth asking whether the relational model still serves every use case.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗼𝗼 𝗳𝗮𝗿

There are clear signals that your data model is no longer fitting comfortably into tables:
• Sparse tables with many unused columns
• Storing JSON or XML because the schema cannot keep up
• Complex many-to-many or deeply nested relationships
• Frequent schema migrations for new types of data
• Write bottlenecks on a single database server
• Growing datasets that are hard to scale vertically

These are often early signs that you may need something beyond the relational world.

𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗹𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗻𝗼𝗻-𝗿𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀

Over the past decade, several database models have emerged to handle new patterns in modern applications:
• Key-value stores for fast lookups and caching
• Document stores for flexible, evolving schemas
• Column-family stores for high-write, large-scale workloads
• Graph databases for deeply connected data
• Distributed key-value systems for massive horizontal scaling

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲

Ask yourself:
• Does my data fit a tabular structure, or is it semi-structured or highly connected
• Do my scaling needs exceed what a single relational instance can deliver
• How much operational complexity can my team manage

Relational databases are not going anywhere, but they are not always the perfect fit. As your application evolves, choosing the right database model can simplify your architecture and improve performance where it matters most.

title: I recently came across an interesting concept in distributed systems called 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗯𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺, and I thought it would be helpful to break it down.

blocks:
I recently came across an interesting concept in distributed systems called 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗯𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺, and I thought it would be helpful to break it down.

Imagine you build a social media platform. For most users, a simple NoSQL setup partitioned by user ID works perfectly. Traffic is balanced and predictable.

But the moment a celebrity joins, everything changes.

Millions of users want to follow them, view their posts, and like content in real time. Suddenly, one partition that was meant for normal traffic starts handling most of the platform’s read and write load. Your backend, which looked evenly distributed on paper, begins to struggle.

Here is how engineering teams usually approach this problem:

𝟭. 𝗔𝗱𝗱 𝗰𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴
A distributed cache like Redis or Memcached serves the frequent reads on celebrity posts. This prevents the hot partition from getting overwhelmed.

𝟮. 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗲 𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴
Reads are manageable with caching, but writes are different. Millions of likes per second cannot hit a single partition.
So you shard the writes. Likes or posts are split across multiple partitions so the workload is distributed horizontally.

𝟯. 𝗨𝗽𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗹𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰
Once sharded, the application needs to know where data resides. To show total likes, it must aggregate counts from different shards. This adds complexity but removes the bottleneck.

𝟰. 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗽𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹-𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗯𝗲𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗼𝗿
Sharding and caching mean working with eventual consistency, building aggregation flows, and routing data intelligently.

𝟱. 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸 𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵 𝗲𝗱𝗴𝗲 𝗰𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀
• What happens if the cache fails
• How you protect the system from sudden write spikes
• How to keep the user experience stable during peak traffic

It is a fascinating problem because systems rarely break at average load. They break when something extraordinary happens, and the Celebrity Problem is the perfect example of designing for those extremes.

title: 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗼 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁?

blocks:
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗶𝘀 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗼 𝗳𝗮𝘀𝘁?

Redis is known for its exceptional speed and low-latency performance, capable of handling over 100,000 queries per second. Its design is optimized for in-memory operations, efficient I/O management, and data structure optimization.

𝟭. 𝗥𝗔𝗠-𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲
Redis stores all data in RAM rather than on disk. Since RAM access times are measured in nanoseconds compared to milliseconds for disk access, Redis can perform read and write operations thousands of times faster than traditional disk-based databases. This eliminates I/O bottlenecks and enables real-time data processing.

𝟮. 𝗜𝗢 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲-𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗱 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Redis uses an event-driven model based on IO multiplexing. Multiple client connections are handled concurrently within a single thread using mechanisms like epoll, kqueue, or select. This avoids the overhead of thread context switching and locking, ensuring predictable performance under high concurrency. The single-threaded event loop processes commands sequentially, maintaining data consistency while maximizing CPU efficiency.

𝟯. 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘇𝗲𝗱 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲𝘀
Redis implements highly efficient, low-level data structures tailored for specific use cases.
 • SDS (Simple Dynamic Strings) for O(1) string length retrieval and pre-allocated buffer management.
 • HashTables and ZipLists for compact and fast key-value storage.
 • SkipLists and IntSets for quick sorted data retrieval and membership checks.
These structures minimize memory fragmentation, reduce reallocation costs, and support constant or logarithmic time complexity for most operations.

In essence, Redis achieves its performance through memory-based storage, non-blocking I/O design, and carefully engineered data structures that together ensure minimal latency and high throughput.

title: Have you ever wondered how apps like Instagram, X, or Google instantly tell you “𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗻” when you sign up?

blocks:
Have you ever wondered how apps like Instagram, X, or Google instantly tell you “𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝗻𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝘆 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗻” when you sign up?

At first glance, it seems like a simple database query. But at the scale of billions of users across the globe, it’s far from simple. Running a direct query every time would overwhelm databases and slow down the entire system.

What actually happens under the hood is a fascinating layered approach:
 • 𝗖𝗮𝗰𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 helps with frequently checked names like “alex” or “john.”
 • 𝗕𝗹𝗼𝗼𝗺 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 act as a lightning-fast probabilistic check, instantly ruling out most usernames without touching the database.
 • 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀 handle the final confirmation when needed.
 • And to make things smarter, 𝗧𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 (Prefix Trees) enable features like autocomplete and instant username suggestions.

This combination is what makes the experience feel instant and seamless, even though trillions of possible checks are happening behind the scenes.

For me, it’s a reminder that what looks like “just a simple feature” often hides some of the most elegant engineering at scale.

What other “small” features do you think hide massive engineering behind the curtain?

title: Scaling backend systems often comes down to how background tasks are handled. Initially, our setup used Flask’s 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗣𝗼𝗼𝗹𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗿, which tied tasks to the web container, lacked retries, and created scalability issues.

blocks:
Scaling backend systems often comes down to how background tasks are handled. Initially, our setup used Flask’s 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗣𝗼𝗼𝗹𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗼𝗿, which tied tasks to the web container, lacked retries, and created scalability issues.

To overcome these challenges, I implemented 𝗖𝗲𝗹𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗥𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘀. This allowed tasks to run independently of Flask, added automatic retries, improved fault tolerance, and enabled horizontal scaling across workers.

The impact was significant:
 • Eliminated task failures during crashes or restarts
 • Improved API responsiveness by offloading heavy background jobs
 • Enabled the system to handle surges in workload by distributing tasks across multiple workers
 • Provided clear monitoring of task lifecycle and errors

The result is a backend that is faster, more reliable, and scalable, ensuring a smoother experience for users and a stronger foundation for future growth.

title: 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗵𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁?

blocks:
𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗵𝗶𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝗔𝗣𝗜 𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁?

You open Postman or your frontend makes a call to /api/v1/user/42.
A few hundred milliseconds later, you get a structured JSON response.

But under the surface, here's the full picture:
𝟭. 𝗗𝗡𝗦 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
The domain name is resolved into an IP address using DNS. This step is crucial in directing your request to the correct server.

𝟮. 𝗥𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴
Once the request reaches the server, the framework (Django, Express, Spring Boot, etc.) checks the HTTP method and URL pattern to route it to the appropriate handler.
Example:
GET /api/v1/user/42 routes to get_user_by_id().

𝟯. 𝗠𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
Before hitting the core logic, middleware processes the request. These layers might handle:
 • Authentication and authorization
 • Logging
 • Rate limiting
 • CORS checks
 • Input sanitization
Middleware ensures that only valid, safe, and authorized requests reach your application logic.

𝟰. 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗟𝗼𝗴𝗶𝗰 / 𝗩𝗶𝗲𝘄 𝗙𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
This is where the actual processing happens:
 • Fetch data from the database
 • Apply business rules
 • Validate inputs
 • Format or serialize the output

This layer must be robust, testable, and free of unnecessary coupling.

𝟱. 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻
The processed data is serialized (often as JSON), assigned an appropriate HTTP status code (like 200, 400, or 404), and wrapped in a response object.
Example:return Response({"name": "Ashmita"}, status=200)

𝟲. 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝘀𝗲 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻
The server sends the HTTP response back to the client over the network. TLS encryption (HTTPS) secures the data during transit.
Client-side rendering or further processing takes place after receiving the response.

𝟳. 𝗕𝗲𝘆𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗶𝗰𝘀
An API isn't just about sending and receiving data. It should also account for:
 • Versioning (/api/v1/)
 • Pagination and filtering
 • Idempotency
 • Error design (consistent structure for error messages)
 • Throttling and performance optimization

𝗙𝗶𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘁 - A well-designed API is not about making the server respond it’s about crafting a reliable, predictable, and secure communication system between two independent systems.

title: You enter your username and password. Hit “Login”, and instantly, you’re inside your dashboard.

blocks:
You enter your username and password. Hit “Login”, and instantly, you’re inside your dashboard.

That seamless experience is backed by a well-structured authentication system using middlewares, JWTs, access control, and secure session handling. These components form the backbone of any secure modern application.

𝟭. 𝗥𝗼𝘂𝘁𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗠𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲
Middleware acts as a gatekeeper before routes are accessed. It checks for:
 • Valid access token
 • Session validity
 • Required permissions
This keeps security checks consistent and the codebase clean.

𝟮. 𝗧𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻-𝗕𝗮𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗔𝘂𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗝𝗪𝗧)
Stateless authentication uses tokens like JWT. The process:
 • Client logs in
 • Server returns a signed token
 • Token is sent with each request
 • Server verifies and decodes user info
Combine short-lived access tokens with refresh tokens for balance.

𝟯. 𝗥𝗲𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵 𝗧𝗼𝗸𝗲𝗻 𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄
Refresh tokens enable silent access token renewal. Best practices:
 • Store them securely (e.g., HTTP-only cookies)
 • Revoke on logout or breach
 • Use rotation to avoid reuse attacks

𝟰. 𝗨𝘀𝗲𝗿 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝗶𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀
Once verified, user info is attached to the request for:
 • Role checks
 • Personalization
 • Logging
This helps keep routes lightweight and secure.

𝟱. 𝗣𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝘃𝘀 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝘃𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗔𝗣𝗜𝘀
Separate APIs clearly:
 • Public: No auth (e.g., blog posts)
 • Private: Auth required (e.g., user data)
Private endpoints must validate tokens and enforce access rules.

𝟲. 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗨𝗫
Security must not disrupt user flow. Ensure:
 • Proper HTTP status codes
 • Graceful token expiry handling
 • Secure but smooth redirects
Avoid exposing sensitive errors or forcing frequent logins.

𝟳. 𝗠𝗶𝗱𝗱𝗹𝗲𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝘀 𝗖𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗿𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲

title: If we had to implement the 𝗹𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 from scratch, how would we even start?

blocks:
If we had to implement the 𝗹𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 from scratch, how would we even start?

This seems like a very basic thing, but it gives a lot of clarity. Let’s find out by checking it step by step.

When the 𝗹𝘀 command is typed into a terminal, it lists the contents of the current directory.

Seems simple on the surface, but what’s happening underneath?

First, the shell parses the command. Then, it hands control to the underlying program that knows how to interact with the filesystem.

Now think, how would a custom version of 𝗹𝘀 know
 • Where to look?
 • What files exist?
 • What to show (hidden files, file types, permissions)?

Let’s break the approach into layers of thought:

𝟭. 𝗜𝗻𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:
Start with the base case - no arguments. The goal is to list the current directory’s contents. So the first task is to figure out what the current directory is.

𝟮. 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗗𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀:
Next, we need to retrieve the list of entries - files, folders, symlinks - everything. That means finding a way to scan or iterate through that directory.

𝟯. 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗙𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴:
Not all entries are shown the same way. Hidden files (starting with .), color-coded outputs, or even just sorting alphabetically are all part of this stage.

𝟰. 𝗔𝗱𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗙𝗹𝗮𝗴𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗢𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀:
Over time, more complexity can be added. For example, ls -a, ls -l, ls -lh, etc. Each flag should trigger a variation in logic, whether to show all files, display detailed metadata, or format sizes in human-readable units.

So even a basic utility like 𝗹𝘀 teaches a lot:
 • How the shell parses commands
 • How programs interact with the filesystem
 • How data is presented to the user

Sometimes, the best way to understand systems is by mentally re-building the tools that are relied on every day.

title: "𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗳𝗲𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗮𝘁 '𝗮𝗽𝗶.𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲.𝗰𝗼𝗺' 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗶𝗻 '𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗱.𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲.𝗰𝗼𝗺' 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗦 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆."

blocks:
"𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗳𝗲𝘁𝗰𝗵 𝗮𝘁 '𝗮𝗽𝗶.𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲.𝗰𝗼𝗺' 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗶𝗻 '𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝗱.𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲.𝗰𝗼𝗺' 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗯𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗯𝘆 𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗦 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝗰𝘆."

This is a common error. Right after deploying frontend and backend separately, everything seems fine… until the browser throws this dreaded message.

𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗦 𝗲𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿.
It may seem as if the browser is unnecessarily blocking progress. But here's what’s actually happening.

𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗦 (𝗖𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀-𝗢𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗶𝗻 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴) 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗯𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘀𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗳𝗲𝗮𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲. Its job is to prevent malicious sites from making unauthorized requests to servers.

Why does it happen? When frontend and backend are hosted on different domains or ports, any API call across these is treated as a cross-origin request. The browser blocks it unless the server explicitly permits it.

𝗣𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁 𝗥𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝘀: Before sending certain types of requests (like those with custom headers or non-simple methods like PUT or DELETE), the browser sends a preflight request using the OPTIONS method to check if the actual request is safe. If the server doesn't respond with appropriate headers, the actual request is never sent.

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘁𝗼 𝗳𝗶𝘅 𝗶𝘁: The backend needs to send the correct CORS headers:
 • 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀-𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹-𝗔𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄-𝗢𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗶𝗻: Specifies which origins are permitted
 • 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀-𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹-𝗔𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄-𝗠𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗼𝗱𝘀: Lists allowed HTTP methods (GET, POST, etc.)
 • 𝗔𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀-𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹-𝗔𝗹𝗹𝗼𝘄-𝗛𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀: Lists allowed custom headers

Frameworks like 𝗘𝘅𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀, 𝗗𝗷𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗼, and 𝗦𝗽𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗕𝗼𝗼𝘁 provide easy ways to handle this:
 • In Express (Node.js), use the cors middleware
 • In Django, use the django-cors-headers package
 • In Spring Boot, configure CORS mappings via annotations or config classes

𝗕𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀:
 • In production, always be specific with allowed origins. Avoid * unless building a public API.
 • Test both simple and preflighted requests.
 • Understand request types. The method and headers influence whether a preflight is triggered.

𝗖𝗢𝗥𝗦 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮 𝗯𝘂𝗴. It's a 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗼𝗹 that exists for good reason. It protects applications and users from cross-site attacks and misuse.

title: Coupon code valid for first 100 users only.

blocks:
Coupon code valid for first 100 users only.

𝗪𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝗹 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲, 𝗿𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁? And just as you are about to complete your payment, you realize you might be the 𝟵𝟴𝘁𝗵, 𝟵𝟵𝘁𝗵, 𝗼𝗿 𝟭𝟬𝟬𝘁𝗵 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿.

But here is where things get interesting.

What if, at that exact moment:
 • One person is entering their 𝗢𝗧𝗣
 • Another has just clicked on 𝗣𝗮𝘆 𝗡𝗼𝘄
 • Someone else is reviewing their cart

Now the real question is: 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁?

Is it the person who clicked first?
Is it the one whose payment gateway processed the transaction faster?
Or is it the person who completed OTP verification before others?

Such situations happen more often than we realize. Whether it is a limited-use coupon, a flash sale on smartphones, or booking tickets for a concert, backend systems face such race conditions daily.

And solving this is not as simple as writing a few conditional statements.

Behind the scenes, the backend has to manage:
 • 𝗔𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗶𝗰 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 to precisely track how many coupons have been claimed, even when hundreds or thousands of people are transacting at the same moment.
 • 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹-𝘁𝗶𝗺𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘆 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 to temporarily hold a coupon or seat while the payment is being processed.
 • 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗰𝘆 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗹, using optimistic or pessimistic locking to ensure fairness without sacrificing performance.
 • 𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝘀𝗮𝗳𝗲𝘁𝘆 to avoid overselling or assigning more coupons than promised.

Every 𝗺𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗻𝘁𝘀. A single wrong decision can lead to 𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗯𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀, or 𝗳𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀.

These are the kinds of real-world problems that make backend development so exciting for me. Designing systems that can handle high-concurrency, real-time allocation challenges is not just about good code; it is about thinking strategically and planning for chaos.

So next time you are racing to grab a discount or a concert ticket, remember this: While you are competing, the backend is too.

Under the hood, solving such race conditions often involves using 𝗺𝘂𝘁𝗲𝘅𝗲𝘀 (𝗺𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗲𝘅𝗰𝗹𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗹𝗼𝗰𝗸𝘀) to ensure that shared counters or resources are not accessed by multiple processes at the same time.

Without proper locking, two users might end up grabbing the same coupon or seat and that's where mutexes help maintain consistency in high-concurrency situations.

blocks:
𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗠𝗮𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 ?

Error handling is not optional. It can never be ignored because unexpected situations always occur in real-world applications, and no one wants their app to break when something goes wrong.

If you’ve used apps like Swiggy, Zomato, or Amazon, you’ve probably noticed how smooth and reliable they feel. That’s not because everything always works perfectly. It’s because these apps are designed to handle failures properly.

In the screenshot below, I searched for a completely random and meaningless input on Swiggy. Instead of crashing or showing a confusing error, Swiggy handled it gracefully with a clear message:
“𝗪𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱𝗻’𝘁 𝗳𝗶𝗻𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝘆 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵.”

This is what proper error handling looks like. The app was ready to deal with the unexpected without failing.

𝗥𝗲𝗮𝗹-𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗹𝗱 𝗘𝘅𝗮𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗱 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴:

 𝟭. 𝗢𝘂𝘁-𝗼𝗳-𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗰𝗸 𝗜𝘁𝗲𝗺 𝗼𝗻 𝗔𝗺𝗮𝘇𝗼𝗻
When a product is marked as "Currently unavailable," Amazon does not let you add it to your cart.
The app does not crash. It simply displays the message:
"This item is currently unavailable."

 𝟮. 𝗠𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗥𝗲𝗾𝘂𝗶𝗿𝗲𝗱 𝗙𝗶𝗲𝗹𝗱𝘀 𝗼𝗻 𝗦𝘄𝗶𝗴𝗴𝘆
Try placing an order without entering your delivery address.
Swiggy does not fail. It prompts you to complete the missing details before proceeding.

𝟯. 𝗙𝗮𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗣𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀
Cancel a payment midway on Swiggy or Amazon.
Instead of freezing or failing, the app shows:
"Payment failed. Please try again."

Even critical failures are handled smoothly.

𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗥𝗼𝗯𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗘𝗿𝗿𝗼𝗿 𝗛𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗜𝘀 𝗘𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹:
 • Prevents sudden crashes and keeps your app stable
 • Improves user experience with clear, helpful message
 • Simplifies debugging with meaningful error logs
 • Protects data integrity in critical systems
 • Prevents security risks by not exposing sensitive system details
 • Reflects engineering maturity by preparing for real-world issues

Always ask these questions while building any feature
 • What could go wrong?
 • Am I handling that situation properly?

blocks:
𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗔𝗿𝗲 𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗥𝗲𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱?

Think of a computer as a machine, like a car engine. On its own, it just sits there. To make it do something, you need to give it instructions.

That’s where programming comes in.

Programming is like writing a recipe that the computer follows step by step. Whether it’s:
 • Showing a website
 • Running a mobile app
 • Calculating your expenses

Every task happens because someone wrote code to tell the computer how to do it.

A simple real-world example:
When you click ‘Pay Now’ on a shopping site, the computer doesn’t automatically know what to do. A programmer wrote the logic behind what happens next i.e. verifying payment, sending confirmation, updating inventory, and more.

At the core:
Computer = Machine
Programming = Instructions for the Machine

It’s as simple and as powerful as that.

If you're starting out, remember:
Computers aren’t “smart” until you tell them what to do.
